Comparing agentic RNA-seq analyses across branches

One airway dataset, ten agentic analyses — how they converged, where they diverged, and how correct they were

Published

September 7, 2026

1 Overview

Every demo/* branch of this repository is an independent agentic analysis of the same dataset — the airway experiment (Himes et al. 2014): human airway smooth-muscle cells from four donors, each sequenced untreated and dexamethasone-treated, quantified with RSEM (~58,735 genes × 8 samples). Each branch was produced by a different person driving an AI coding agent toward the same goal: differential expression, Dexamethasone vs Untreated.

This report compares ten of those branches (all except yangz, which is data-only) across the three artefacts the agents produced — the CLAUDE.md context file, the analysis script, and the results — and assesses how correct each analysis was against an independent, published reference.

Method in one paragraph

We re-ran every branch we could from source (R/DESeq2 via knitr::purl; PyDESeq2 in a Python 3.12 env; clawbio branches from their committed output, since the clawbio engine was not available here), harmonized each DE table to a common schema, and scored them against a gold-standard reference: the canonical DESeq2 workflow on the published Bioconductor airway package (~ cell + dex, Untreated reference, apeglm shrinkage) — deliberately a different quantification than this repo’s RSEM matrix, so concordance is judged on rank, overlap, direction and marker recovery rather than absolute fold-change. All numbers below are computed by the harness in analysis/harness/ and read from analysis/data/.

2 Layer 1 — the CLAUDE.md context files

The CLAUDE.md is the context each agent was given (or wrote) about the dataset. We scored each against a fixed 16-point rubric of correct, analysis-critical facts, by objective keyword presence.

Consensus. Ten out of ten correctly identify the dataset, state the analysis language/deliverable convention, note that the two files join on sample ID (not position), and flag that the transcript_id(s) column must be dropped. The paired design and the ~ cellLine + treatment formula are near-universal (9/10 and 8/10).

Divergence. The files split sharply on the measured details that separate a generic dataset description from an analysis-ready brief:

  • Pre-filtering is mentioned by only 3/10 (tiph, pateld1, marga).
  • Marker genes for a biological sanity check and library-size variation appear in only 2/10 (tiph, marga).
  • The sign-flip risk from R’s alphabetical factor default is warned about in 4/10.

Accuracy. Every quantitative claim we could check was correct: the branches that cite measured numbers (tiph, marga, pateld1) state 58,735 genes, 28,344 all-zero (48.3%), 11,117 non-integer rows, and 14.9–30.3 M library sizes — all verified exactly against the data. No CLAUDE.md contained a false statement; the differences are of depth, not accuracy. The files that “measured the data” (tiph, marga, pateld1) produced richer briefs — but, as Layer 2 shows, the leaner briefs still yielded correct analyses, because the omitted facts (round, filter, reference level) are also DESeq2 standard practice and were applied in code regardless.

The consensus recipe. Independently, all ten converged on the same statistically-correct pipeline:

  1. Design ~ cellLine + treatment — the paired/blocked design, in every branch. None fell into the “4-vs-4 unpaired” trap that was flagged as the most likely mistake.
  2. Untreated as reference — set explicitly everywhere (via relevel, explicit factor levels, category reorder, or clawbio’s contrast direction), so a positive LFC = induced.
  3. Round RSEM counts to integers before modelling.
  4. Low-count pre-filter, then apeglm/clawbio LFC shrinkage, BH-adjusted p-values at padj < 0.05, and VST for PCA/clustering.
  5. The full diagnostic suite — PCA, volcano, MA, sample-distance, and expression heatmaps appear in nearly every branch.

Where they diverged (all defensible):

  • Engine. Seven used R/DESeq2; pateld1 used PyDESeq2; barretj and davidlvb used the clawbio skill (a PyDESeq2 wrapper). This is the single biggest split and the one visible in the outputs (Layer 3).
  • Low-count filter. Total-count ≥ 10 (Catarina, marga, okp-23, pateld1) vs ≥ 10 in ≥ 4 samples (Olivia, santosnuno, becky, tiph) vs ≥ 10 in ≥ 2 (davidlvb) vs clawbio’s default (barretj). This changes genes tested substantially but significant genes barely (Layer 3).
  • Symbol mapping. All but becky map Ensembl IDs to symbols (becky stays in Ensembl IDs).
  • Scope & polish. davidlvb alone adds pathway enrichment; okp-23 ships reusable skills with unit tests; pateld1 adds a paired-vs-unpaired sensitivity check and assertion guards; barretj ships a full reproducibility bundle; tiph/marga invest in report styling.

Correctness review. Reading every script, we found no correctness-breaking bug: no dropped blocking factor, no mis-set reference, no floor()/truncation of counts. Two branches show notable defensive engineering — pateld1 encodes every consistency check as a runtime assertion (and handles the PyDESeq2 0.5.x reference-level API), and tiph degrades gracefully from apeglm to normal shrinkage if apeglm is absent. davidlvb documents a real clawbio Enrichr bug and works around it with gseapy.

4 Layer 3 — the results

4.1 Genes tested vs significant

The low-count filter is the most visible methodological choice, yet DESeq2’s independent filtering absorbs most of it: R/DESeq2 branches call 3,917–3,950 significant genes regardless of filter, while the PyDESeq2 (pateld1, 3,629) and clawbio (barretj, 3,662) engines run slightly more conservative.

4.2 Cross-branch agreement

On the shared RSEM matrix the branches are almost indistinguishable: median pairwise Spearman LFC = 1.00, median significant-set Jaccard = 0.955. barretj (clawbio) is the only mild outlier (0.96–0.98), reflecting its different filter and engine. 3,491 genes are significant in all nine quantitatively-compared branches — and 94% of that core set is also significant in the independent airway reference.

4.3 Concordance with the published reference

Against a different quantification of the same experiment, every branch lands at Pearson LFC 0.90–0.97 and top-100 overlap 0.86–0.93. The ≥10-in-≥4-samples branches (becky, Olivia, santosnuno, tiph) correlate best (0.967) — a slightly stricter filter drops noisy low-count genes and tightens agreement with the reference.

4.4 Biological validity

This is the strongest evidence that all agents recovered the correct biology: for the known responders, every branch reproduces the reference log2FC to within rounding (SPARCL1 ≈ 4.6, ZBTB16 ≈ 7.3, KLF15 ≈ 4.4, DUSP1 ≈ 3.0), and CCL2 is repressed everywhere. Direction agreement with the reference on co-significant genes is 100% in every branch.

Every branch is statistically and biologically correct (A, B, C at ceiling). Branches separate almost entirely on reproducibility (E) and marginally on concordance (D). barretj leads on the strength of a full reproducibility bundle (checksums, pinned environment, replayable commands); pateld1 follows (assertions, pinned requirements, seed); the tightly-filtered R branches (tiph, Olivia, santosnuno, becky) score highest on concordance. davidlvb’s C/D are n/a (its clawbio output could not be regenerated here); its method mirrors barretj.

6 Consensus vs divergence — the bottom line

Consensus (what every agent got right). Same dataset understanding, same paired design, same reference level, same core statistical recipe, and — most importantly — the same answer: a ~3,500-gene core DE set, recovered in every branch, 94% of it confirmed by an independent published reference, with all known glucocorticoid markers induced in the correct direction. The agentic analyses are reproducible and correct, and they agree with each other to a near-perfect degree.

Divergence (where taste and tooling showed). The differences are real but sit above the statistics: choice of engine (R/DESeq2 vs PyDESeq2 vs clawbio — the only choice that visibly moved the significant-gene count), filter stringency (shifts genes-tested, not conclusions), symbol annotation, and how far past core DE each went — enrichment (davidlvb), reusable tested skills (okp-23), reproducibility rigor (barretj, pateld1), sensitivity analysis (pateld1), and report polish (tiph, marga). The CLAUDE.md files varied most of all (6/16 to 16/16 coverage), yet that variance did not propagate to the results — the standard-practice steps some briefs omitted were applied in code anyway.

How correct were they? Uniformly correct. No branch made a design or statistical error that changed the biology. The spread that remains is a spread in engineering quality and scope, not in scientific validity.

Caveats & limitations

  • Reference quantification differs. The airway package’s counts come from a different pipeline than this repo’s RSEM matrix, so we weight rank/overlap/direction/marker recovery over absolute LFC. Cross-branch agreement (all on the identical RSEM matrix) is the tighter, secondary anchor and shows near-perfect consensus.
  • Best-effort execution. barretj is compared from committed clawbio output and davidlvb from source only (clawbio/uvx unavailable in this environment). The eight re-run branches reproduce their committed results where those exist (e.g. becky’s 3,950 significant genes).
  • Harvesting. For R branches without a committed results CSV, an additive, export-only step serialised the branch’s own final results object — no statistical step was reimplemented or altered.
  • Rubric subjectivity. Layer-1 coverage and the reproducibility dimension (E) are reviewer rubrics; Layers 2–3 (methods, correlations, overlaps, marker recovery) are objective.
Reproduce this report

analysis/harness/ holds the full pipeline: install_bioc.R → build_reference.R → materialize.sh → run_r_branch.R (+ PyDESeq2 env for pateld1) → compute_metrics.R → score_claudemd.R → build_scorecard.R → make_figures.R, then render this .qmd.
